title: British National Grid Helper: BNG Conversions
description: Work between GPS coordinates and British National Grid references with the British National Grid Helper — grid letters and figures explained. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, London sits in the TQ 100-kilometre square — two letters that narrow a GPS point to one square of Britain before a single digit is read.
quick_answer: The British National Grid Helper supports UK coordinate workflows between GPS latitude/longitude and National Grid style values. Grid references combine two letters naming a 100-kilometre square with digits that refine the point inside it — four figures to a kilometre, six to 100 metres, ten to a metre.

body.t: Ordnance Survey maps speak grid references. Convert a GPS point to its reference before quoting it to a walking group — the group will navigate by it.
British officialdom asks for grid references. The helper bridges between the GPS world and the form's expectation.
Finds and sites are logged by grid reference in UK practice — the museum-grade habit starts with a correct conversion.
The two-letter square system (SV in the far southwest up to TA, TQ for London, and the rest) becomes obvious once you convert a few home points.

A 4-figure reference names a 1 km square; 6 figures, 100 m; 8 figures, 10 m; 10 figures, 1 m. Each added pair of digits divides the square by ten in each direction — the ladder every UK walker climbs unconsciously.

The National Grid rides on OSGB36, not WGS84. The same ground point carries different coordinates in the two — differing by up to roughly a hundred metres across Britain — which is why 'full OSGB36?' is this page's first FAQ.

faq: Is it full OSGB36?

The helper supports National Grid style workflows; rigorous OSGB36 transformation (the OSTN-class shift) is Ordnance Survey's own product. For walking, forms and general work the helper's level is the working standard — survey law wants the official transformation.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
This family's default is WGS84; the British grid is OSGB36 — the page exists because Britain is the exception, and the difference is stated rather than hidden.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
In grid terms: more figures mean a smaller square, not a truer point. A 10-figure reference from a 5-metre GPS fix is precision theatre.
Can I copy the result into GIS software?
Yes — grid references and coordinates both paste into GIS; set the layer's CRS to OSGB36 (EPSG:27700) for grid values so the software honours the datum.
Why two letters and not one?
The letters encode two nested squares (500 km, then 100 km) in a scheme designed before computers — compact, pronounceable, and unambiguous across Britain.
Northern Ireland?
It uses the Irish Grid (and modern ITM) — a separate system with its own helper page on this site.
The letters skip I — why?
To avoid confusion with the digit 1. A small kindness from the grid's designers that every recorder of references appreciates.
Can I convert a reference back to GPS?
The workflow runs both ways — reference to coordinates for the GPS, coordinates to reference for the map and the form.
Offshore points?
The grid extends over coastal waters in its projection, but references are a land habit; at sea, latitude/longitude rules.
Historic references?
Old references may ride older county series or the pre-grid systems; the modern National Grid dates from the 1936 retriangulation onward.
What precision should I quote?
Match the source: a phone fix earns 6 or 8 figures. Quoting 10 from a 5-metre fix misleads the reader about the point's certainty.
